prompt: The law of demand states that, all else equal, there is a(n) ___ relationship between the price of a good and the quantity demanded.

options.label: A
options.text: Proportional — a 10% rise in price always causes a 10% rise in quantity demanded

options.label: B
options.text: Inverse — as price rises, quantity demanded falls

options.label: C
options.text: Neutral — price and quantity demanded do not affect each other

options.label: D
options.text: Direct — as price rises, quantity demanded rises

options.label: E
options.text: Positive — as price rises, quantity demanded rises

explanation: The law of demand describes an inverse (negative) relationship between price and quantity demanded: when price rises, consumers buy less; when price falls, consumers buy more, all else equal.

prompt: Which of the following best describes the shape of a demand curve on a standard price-quantity graph?

options.label: A
options.text: U-shaped, reflecting diminishing and then increasing demand

options.label: B
options.text: Upward-sloping from left to right

options.label: C
options.text: A horizontal line at the market price

options.label: D
options.text: Downward-sloping from left to right

options.label: E
options.text: A vertical line at the equilibrium quantity

explanation: The law of demand implies a downward-sloping demand curve: as price falls (moving down the vertical axis), quantity demanded increases (moving right along the horizontal axis).

prompt: When the price of coffee rises from $3 to $5 per cup, consumers purchase fewer cups per week. This outcome best illustrates

options.label: A
options.text: A movement upward along demand as quantity demanded falls

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in consumer income that reduces demand

options.label: C
options.text: A rightward shift of the demand curve for coffee

options.label: D
options.text: A change in consumer preferences away from coffee

options.label: E
options.text: A leftward shift of the demand curve for coffee

explanation: A change in the price of a good causes a movement along the existing demand curve - not a shift of the curve. Here, a higher price leads consumers to buy fewer cups, which is a decrease in quantity demanded (a movement up and to the left along the curve).

prompt: A change in which of the following causes a movement along the demand curve rather than a shift of the demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumer income

options.label: B
options.text: The price of a related good

options.label: C
options.text: The number of buyers in the market

options.label: D
options.text: The price of the good itself

options.label: E
options.text: Consumer tastes and preferences

explanation: Only a change in the price of the good itself causes a movement along the demand curve (a change in quantity demanded). All other factors - income, prices of related goods, tastes, number of buyers, expectations - are determinants that shift the entire demand curve.

prompt: Which of the following would cause the demand curve for pizza to shift to the right?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in the number of pizza producers

options.label: B
options.text: A decrease in the price of pizza

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the cost of pizza ingredients

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in consumer income, if pizza is a normal good

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in the price of pizza

explanation: A determinant of demand - such as a rise in consumer income (when the good is normal) - shifts the demand curve. An increase in income increases consumers' willingness and ability to buy pizza at every price, shifting demand rightward; price changes cause movements along the curve, not shifts.

prompt: A normal good is best defined as a good for which

options.label: A
options.text: Demand decreases when consumer income increases

options.label: B
options.text: The price is always above the market equilibrium

options.label: C
options.text: The quantity supplied is always constant

options.label: D
options.text: Demand increases when consumer income increases

options.label: E
options.text: The price rises when consumer income rises

explanation: A normal good has a positive income-demand relationship: when consumer income rises, demand for the good increases (the demand curve shifts right); most goods are normal goods.

prompt: An inferior good is best defined as a good for which

options.label: A
options.text: The good lacks close substitutes

options.label: B
options.text: Its price is below equilibrium

options.label: C
options.text: Consumers prefer more at every price

options.label: D
options.text: Demand increases when income rises

options.label: E
options.text: Demand decreases when consumer income rises

explanation: An inferior good has a negative income-demand relationship: when consumer income rises, consumers buy less of the inferior good, shifting its demand curve leftward; examples include generic staples and some forms of public transit.

prompt: Two goods are substitutes if

options.label: A
options.text: A rise in consumer income increases demand for both goods simultaneously

options.label: B
options.text: A rise in the price of one good leads to a decrease in the demand for the other good

options.label: C
options.text: A higher price for one increases demand for the other

options.label: D
options.text: They are produced using the same factors of production

options.label: E
options.text: They are always consumed together, such as peanut butter and jelly

explanation: Substitute goods compete with each other to satisfy the same consumer need; when the price of one rises, it becomes relatively more expensive, so consumers switch to the substitute - increasing demand for the substitute good.

prompt: Two goods are complements if

options.label: A
options.text: A rise in the price of one good leads to an increase in the demand for the other good

options.label: B
options.text: A higher price for one decreases demand for the other

options.label: C
options.text: Their prices always move in the same direction

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in consumer income reduces demand for both goods

options.label: E
options.text: They compete with each other to satisfy the same consumer want

explanation: Complementary goods are consumed together; when the price of one rises, consumers buy less of it - and since both are used together, demand for the complement also falls; examples include cars and gasoline, or printers and ink cartridges.

prompt: If the price of hot dogs rises significantly, what would most likely happen to the demand for hot dog buns, assuming they are complements?

options.label: A
options.text: Bun demand rises through substitution

options.label: B
options.text: Bun demand stays unchanged; goods are separate

options.label: C
options.text: Bun demand rises with income

options.label: D
options.text: Bun demand falls as hot-dog consumption falls

options.label: E
options.text: Bun demand rises as relative prices fall

explanation: Hot dogs and hot dog buns are complements - consumed together; when the price of hot dogs rises, consumers buy fewer hot dogs, which reduces the demand for buns as well; the demand curve for hot dog buns shifts left.

prompt: If the price of Pepsi rises substantially, what would most likely happen to the demand for Coca-Cola, assuming they are substitutes?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for Coca-Cola would decrease because both products are similar

options.label: B
options.text: Demand for Coca-Cola would increase because some Pepsi consumers switch to Coca-Cola

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for Coca-Cola would increase because its production costs fell

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for Coca-Cola would decrease because consumer income fell

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for Coca-Cola would remain unchanged because they are different brands

explanation: When the price of Pepsi (a substitute for Coke) rises, Pepsi becomes relatively more expensive; some consumers switch to Coca-Cola, increasing demand for Coke; the demand curve for Coca-Cola shifts rightward.

prompt: Which of the following is a determinant of demand that can shift the demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: The wages paid to workers who produce the good

options.label: B
options.text: The cost of inputs used to produce the good

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer income

options.label: D
options.text: The quantity of the good being produced

options.label: E
options.text: The price of the good being demanded

explanation: Consumer income is a determinant of demand - a non-price factor that, when it changes, shifts the entire demand curve. The price of the good itself only causes a movement along the existing curve; input costs and wages are supply-side factors.

prompt: A leftward shift of the demand curve indicates that consumers are now willing and able to buy

options.label: A
options.text: More of the good because the price fell

options.label: B
options.text: More of the good at every price level

options.label: C
options.text: The same amount but at a higher price

options.label: D
options.text: Less of the good at every price level

options.label: E
options.text: More of the good only at lower prices

explanation: A leftward (inward) shift of the demand curve means that at every given price, consumers demand a smaller quantity than before; this represents a decrease in demand caused by a change in a demand determinant.

prompt: A rightward shift of the demand curve indicates that consumers are now willing and able to buy

options.label: A
options.text: More of the good at every price level

options.label: B
options.text: Less of the good because income fell

options.label: C
options.text: The same quantity but at a lower price

options.label: D
options.text: Less of the good at every price level

options.label: E
options.text: The same amount of the good regardless of price

explanation: A rightward (outward) shift of the demand curve means that at every given price, consumers demand a greater quantity than before; this represents an increase in demand caused by a change in a non-price determinant.

prompt: Which of the following events would most likely cause the demand curve for new cars to shift leftward?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in the price of new cars

options.label: B
options.text: An improvement in consumer preferences for cars over public transit

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the number of new car buyers entering the market

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in consumer income

options.label: E
options.text: A decrease in consumer income, assuming cars are a normal good

explanation: New cars are a normal good - demand rises with income and falls when income decreases; A decrease in consumer income reduces consumers' ability to buy new cars, shifting the demand curve leftward.

prompt: Which of the following would cause the demand curve for bus rides (an inferior good) to shift rightward?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in the price of bus rides

options.label: B
options.text: A decrease in consumer income

options.label: C
options.text: An improvement in consumer preferences for private cars

options.label: D
options.text: An increase in the price of bus rides

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in consumer income

explanation: Bus rides are an inferior good - demand increases when consumer income falls; when income decreases, consumers are less able to afford private cars and turn to cheaper alternatives like buses, shifting demand for bus rides rightward.

prompt: A change in consumer tastes and preferences in favor of a good will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Cause a movement up the demand curve

options.label: B
options.text: Have no effect on the demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: Shift the demand curve to the right

options.label: D
options.text: Shift the demand curve to the left

options.label: E
options.text: Cause a movement down the demand curve

explanation: Consumer tastes and preferences are a determinant of demand; when consumers develop a stronger preference for a good, they want to buy more of it at every price - shifting the demand curve rightward.

prompt: If the number of buyers in a market increases significantly, the demand curve for that good will most likely

options.label: A
options.text: Shift rightward because total market demand increases

options.label: B
options.text: Flattens because demand becomes more elastic

options.label: C
options.text: Stays unchanged because individual demand is unaffected

options.label: D
options.text: Steepens because demand becomes more inelastic

options.label: E
options.text: Shifts left because buyers increase competition

explanation: The number of buyers is a determinant of market demand; more buyers mean greater total demand for the good at every price level, shifting the market demand curve rightward.

prompt: Consumers expect the price of laptops to rise significantly next month. How will this expectation most likely affect the current demand for laptops?

options.label: A
options.text: Current demand falls while consumers await higher prices

options.label: B
options.text: Current demand is unchanged; expectations have no effect

options.label: C
options.text: Current demand rises in anticipation of higher future prices

options.label: D
options.text: Current demand rises because future prices are lower

options.label: E
options.text: Current demand falls because future income is uncertain

explanation: Consumer expectations about future prices are a determinant of current demand; if consumers expect prices to rise, they have an incentive to buy now rather than later, increasing current demand and shifting the demand curve rightward.

prompt: The market demand curve for a good is derived by

options.label: A
options.text: Subtracting the lowest individual demand from the highest

options.label: B
options.text: Multiplying each consumer's demand by the market price

options.label: C
options.text: Choosing the individual demand curve of the median consumer

options.label: D
options.text: Summing the quantities demanded by all individual consumers at each price level

options.label: E
options.text: Averaging the individual demand curves of all consumers

explanation: The market demand curve is obtained by horizontally summing all individual demand curves - that is, adding up the quantities each consumer demands at every given price; this gives total market quantity demanded at each price.

prompt: A demand schedule shows that as the price of a hamburger falls from $8 to $6, the quantity demanded rises from 100 to 140 per day. This relationship is consistent with

options.label: A
options.text: An upward-sloping demand curve, showing a positive price-quantity relationship

options.label: B
options.text: A movement along the supply curve

options.label: C
options.text: A shift in the demand curve caused by a change in consumer income

options.label: D
options.text: The inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded

options.label: E
options.text: A shift in the demand curve caused by a change in consumer tastes

explanation: As price falls from $8 to $6, quantity demanded rises from 100 to 140 - price and quantity move in opposite directions; this is consistent with the law of demand, which states an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded.

prompt: Which of the following correctly distinguishes between a "change in demand" and a "change in quantity demanded"?

options.label: A
options.text: Both own-price and income changes shift demand

options.label: B
options.text: Own-price changes affect supply; income changes affect neither

options.label: C
options.text: Own-price changes shift demand; income changes cause movements

options.label: D
options.text: Own-price changes cause movements; income changes shift demand

options.label: E
options.text: Both own-price and income changes cause movements

explanation: A change in quantity demanded is caused by a change in the good's own price - it is a movement along the existing demand curve. A change in demand is caused by a change in a non-price determinant (income, preferences, related goods prices, etc.) - it shifts the entire demand curve.

prompt: Peanut butter and jelly are complementary goods. If the price of peanut butter rises significantly, what happens to the demand for jelly?

options.label: A
options.text: Jelly demand falls as its complement becomes more expensive

options.label: B
options.text: Demand for jelly decreases because consumer income falls

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for jelly increases because consumers substitute toward jelly

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for jelly is unaffected because jelly has its own separate price

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for jelly increases because jelly becomes relatively cheaper

explanation: Peanut butter and jelly are complements - they are used together; A higher price for peanut butter reduces purchases of peanut butter, which simultaneously reduces the demand for jelly; the demand curve for jelly shifts leftward.

prompt: Which of the following is NOT a determinant of demand that shifts the demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumer expectations about future prices

options.label: B
options.text: The price of the good itself

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer income

options.label: D
options.text: The price of a substitute good

options.label: E
options.text: Consumer tastes and preferences

explanation: The price of the good itself does not shift the demand curve - it causes a movement along the existing demand curve (a change in quantity demanded). All other listed factors are non-price determinants that, when changed, shift the demand curve.

prompt: A consumer's individual demand curve for pizza shows the quantity of pizza the consumer is willing and able to purchase

options.label: A
options.text: When all other consumers' incomes are held constant

options.label: B
options.text: At a single fixed income level and fixed price

options.label: C
options.text: At various prices, all else equal

options.label: D
options.text: When the consumer's income rises

options.label: E
options.text: At the market equilibrium price only

explanation: An individual demand curve shows the relationship between the price of the good and the quantity the consumer is willing and able to buy, holding all other factors (income, preferences, related goods prices) constant.

prompt: A health study is released showing that consuming a particular brand of chips causes significant health problems. As a result, what happens to the demand for those chips?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand is unaffected because the price has not changed

options.label: B
options.text: Demand increases because the chips become rarer

options.label: C
options.text: Demand increases because consumers are more aware of the product

options.label: D
options.text: Demand decreases only if the price also rises

options.label: E
options.text: Demand decreases as consumer preferences shift away from the chips

explanation: Consumer tastes and preferences are a determinant of demand; negative information about a product (e.g., health risks) shifts consumer preferences away from it, decreasing demand and shifting the demand curve leftward.

prompt: The price of tea falls significantly. Tea and coffee are substitutes. What happens to the demand for coffee?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for coffee decreases because tea becomes a relatively cheaper substitute

options.label: B
options.text: Demand for coffee decreases because consumer income fell

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for coffee remains the same because coffee has its own price

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for coffee increases because tea and coffee are substitutes

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for coffee increases because the price of coffee fell

explanation: Tea and coffee are substitutes; when the price of tea falls, tea becomes cheaper relative to coffee, so some consumers switch from coffee to tea; the demand for coffee decreases - its demand curve shifts leftward.

prompt: Two buyers — Ana and Ben — have the following individual demands for apples at $1 per apple: Ana demands 4 apples; Ben demands 6 apples. What is the total market quantity demanded at $1?

options.label: A
options.text: 6 apples

options.label: B
options.text: 5 apples

options.label: C
options.text: 24 apples

options.label: D
options.text: 4 apples

options.label: E
options.text: 10 apples

explanation: Market demand at any price is the horizontal sum of individual demands; at $1: Ana (4) + Ben (6) = 10 apples total market quantity demanded.

prompt: Consumer expectations that a good's price will FALL in the near future would most likely cause current demand for that good to

options.label: A
options.text: Decrease, because consumers will wait to buy at the lower future price

options.label: B
options.text: Increase, because lower future prices signal higher quality

options.label: C
options.text: Increase, because consumers expect to save money

options.label: D
options.text: Decrease, because income uncertainty causes saving

options.label: E
options.text: Remain unchanged, because current prices are what matter

explanation: When consumers expect prices to fall, they have an incentive to delay purchases and wait for the lower future price; this reduces current demand, shifting the demand curve leftward.

prompt: Which of the following scenarios describes a movement along the demand curve for gasoline rather than a shift of the curve?

options.label: A
options.text: The price of electric vehicles falls, causing consumers to switch away from gasoline cars

options.label: B
options.text: Consumer income rises, increasing the quantity of gasoline demanded at every price

options.label: C
options.text: The price of gasoline rises, causing consumers to purchase less gasoline

options.label: D
options.text: A new highway is opened, increasing the number of commuters who drive

options.label: E
options.text: Electric vehicles become more popular, reducing the preference for gasoline

explanation: A change in the price of gasoline itself causes a movement along the existing demand curve - not a shift; when price rises, quantity demanded falls (law of demand).

prompt: If beef and chicken are substitutes, and the price of beef rises, which of the following most accurately describes the effect on the demand for chicken?

options.label: A
options.text: The demand for chicken decreases because consumer preferences shifted away from meat

options.label: B
options.text: The demand for chicken decreases because beef and chicken are consumed together

options.label: C
options.text: The quantity demanded of chicken remains the same because chicken's own price did not change

options.label: D
options.text: Chicken demand rises as consumers substitute away from beef

options.label: E
options.text: The quantity demanded of chicken decreases because consumers have less income to spend

explanation: Beef and chicken are substitutes; when beef becomes more expensive, some consumers switch to chicken as a cheaper alternative; this increases the demand for chicken - the demand curve for chicken shifts rightward.

prompt: On a demand graph, what does a movement from a point on the demand curve to a new point further down (and to the right) along the same curve represent?

options.label: A
options.text: A decrease in demand due to a fall in consumer preferences

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in demand due to higher consumer income

options.label: C
options.text: A shift of the demand curve to the left

options.label: D
options.text: A shift of the demand curve to the right

options.label: E
options.text: Greater quantity demanded at a lower price

explanation: A movement down and to the right along the same demand curve represents an increase in quantity demanded caused by a decrease in the good's own price. The demand curve itself has not changed - only the price-quantity position has moved.
graphDescription: Downward-sloping demand curve with price on vertical axis and quantity demanded on horizontal axis. Point A is at a higher price and lower quantity; Point B is at a lower price and higher quantity. An arrow shows a movement from A to B along the same demand curve.

prompt: If consumer income increases and the good is a normal good, which of the following best describes the graphical change to the demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: There is a movement up the existing demand curve

options.label: B
options.text: The demand curve shifts leftward, showing less quantity demanded at every price

options.label: C
options.text: The demand curve shifts rightward, showing more quantity demanded at every price

options.label: D
options.text: There is a movement down the existing demand curve

options.label: E
options.text: The demand curve rotates clockwise, becoming steeper

explanation: For a normal good, an increase in consumer income increases demand - consumers are willing and able to buy more at every price; this is represented as a rightward shift of the entire demand curve.

prompt: The demand schedule for movie tickets is as follows: At $5, 200 tickets demanded; at $8, 150 tickets; at $11, 100 tickets; at $14, 50 tickets. A new streaming service launches and significantly reduces the appeal of movie theaters. Which of the following best describes what happens to this demand schedule?

options.label: A
options.text: The schedule is unchanged; only the supply of tickets is affected by streaming

options.label: B
options.text: The quantities demanded at each price increase, and the demand curve shifts rightward

options.label: C
options.text: The price column changes, reflecting higher ticket prices due to competition

options.label: D
options.text: Less demand at every price; the curve shifts left

options.label: E
options.text: There is a movement along the demand curve to a lower quantity at the same price

explanation: The launch of a competing streaming service changes consumer preferences and the availability of substitutes for movie-going. This is a non-price determinant change that decreases demand: fewer tickets are demanded at every price; the demand curve shifts leftward.

prompt: A graph shows two demand curves: D₁ and D₂, where D₂ is to the right of D₁. Which of the following events would best explain a shift from D₁ to D₂ for organic vegetables?

options.label: A
options.text: A blight reduces the available supply of organic vegetables

options.label: B
options.text: Research improves consumers' preferences for organic vegetables

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer income decreases and organic vegetables are a normal good

options.label: D
options.text: The number of organic vegetable producers decreases

options.label: E
options.text: The price of organic vegetables decreases

explanation: A rightward shift from D₁ to D₂ represents an increase in demand. A positive health study shifts consumer preferences strongly in favor of organic vegetables, increasing the amount demanded at every price; this is a change in consumer tastes - a demand determinant.
graphDescription: Price-quantity graph with two downward-sloping demand curves. D₁ is the original curve, D₂ is to the right of D₁, indicating greater quantity demanded at every price. Both axes are labeled: price (vertical) and quantity of organic vegetables (horizontal).

prompt: Consumer income rises. Which of the following correctly pairs the type of good with the resulting shift of its demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Normal good: demand shifts right; Inferior good: demand shifts left

options.label: B
options.text: Normal good: demand shifts left; Inferior good: demand shifts left

options.label: C
options.text: Normal good: demand shifts right; Inferior good: demand shifts right

options.label: D
options.text: Both types of goods experience a movement along the curve, not a shift

options.label: E
options.text: Normal good: demand shifts left; Inferior good: demand shifts right

explanation: For normal goods, higher income increases demand (rightward shift); for inferior goods, higher income decreases demand (leftward shift), because consumers can now afford preferred, higher-quality alternatives.

prompt: The price of printer ink cartridges rises sharply. Printers and ink cartridges are complements. Which of the following best describes the effect on the demand for printers?

options.label: A
options.text: Printer quantity demanded falls along its demand curve

options.label: B
options.text: Printer demand rises because printers become relatively cheaper

options.label: C
options.text: Printer demand rises because ink is consumed with printers

options.label: D
options.text: Printer demand stays unchanged because printer prices are fixed

options.label: E
options.text: Printer demand falls as complementary ink becomes more expensive

explanation: Printers and ink cartridges are complements. A rise in ink cartridge prices raises the total cost of printer ownership; this reduces the appeal of printers, decreasing demand for printers and shifting the printer demand curve leftward.

prompt: Gasoline and SUVs are complements. The price of gasoline falls substantially. Which of the following describes the most likely effect on the demand for SUVs?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for SUVs falls because consumers spend less on gasoline and save instead

options.label: B
options.text: The quantity demanded of SUVs falls due to a movement along the SUV demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for SUVs falls because cheaper gasoline shifts consumer preferences toward smaller cars

options.label: D
options.text: SUV demand rises as complementary gasoline becomes cheaper

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for SUVs is unaffected because the price of SUVs did not change

explanation: SUVs and gasoline are complements; when gasoline prices fall, the cost of driving an SUV decreases, making SUVs more attractive; this increases the demand for SUVs, shifting the SUV demand curve rightward.

prompt: Three individual demand schedules for apples at $2 per apple: Consumer 1 buys 3; Consumer 2 buys 5; Consumer 3 buys 2. At $3 per apple: Consumer 1 buys 2; Consumer 2 buys 3; Consumer 3 buys 1. What is the total market quantity demanded at each price?

options.label: A
options.text: At $2: 10 apples; At $3: 5 apples

options.label: B
options.text: At $2: 8 apples; At $3: 5 apples

options.label: C
options.text: At $2: 3 apples; At $3: 1 apple

options.label: D
options.text: At $2: 5 apples; At $3: 2 apples

options.label: E
options.text: At $2: 10 apples; At $3: 6 apples

explanation: Market demand = sum of all individual demands at each price; at $2: 3+5+2 = 10 apples; at $3: 2+3+1 = 6 apples; this horizontal summation gives the market demand schedule.

prompt: Using the data from the previous question (market demand: 10 at $2; 6 at $3), a fourth consumer enters the market who demands 4 apples at $2 and 3 at $3. What is the new total market quantity demanded?

options.label: D
options.text: At $2: 10; At $3: 6 (unchanged)

explanation: Adding a new buyer increases market demand; new totals: At $2: 10 + 4 = 14. At $3: 6 + 3 = 9; the entry of a new buyer shifts the market demand curve rightward at every price.

prompt: Butter and margarine are substitutes. The price of margarine rises significantly. Independently, consumer income also rises. Butter is a normal good. What happens to the demand for butter as a result of BOTH changes?

options.label: A
options.text: The quantity demanded of butter increases due to a price movement

options.label: B
options.text: Demand for butter is unaffected because the effects cancel out

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for butter decreases due to both changes

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for butter increases due to both changes

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for butter decreases due to the income change only

explanation: Two separate forces both increase the demand for butter: (1) higher margarine prices make butter relatively cheaper, driving substitution toward butter; (2) higher consumer income increases demand for butter (a normal good). Both determinants shift the butter demand curve rightward.

prompt: A large number of baby boomers retire and move to Florida, increasing the population of elderly residents. Florida's market for retirement community housing is affected. Which of the following best explains the impact on housing demand?

options.label: A
options.text: A rightward shift because retirees are wealthier than younger buyers

options.label: B
options.text: A leftward shift of the demand curve due to fewer working-age adults

options.label: C
options.text: A movement along the demand curve as housing prices rise

options.label: D
options.text: No change in demand because housing is an inferior good for retirees

options.label: E
options.text: A rightward shift due to more potential buyers

explanation: An increase in the number of buyers in a market is a demand determinant. More retirees moving to Florida increases the number of buyers in the retirement housing market, shifting demand rightward - more housing is demanded at every price.

prompt: A consumer's demand curve for a good shifts leftward after a recession reduces her income by 30%. Before the recession, she bought 8 units at $10 per unit. After the income loss, she buys only 5 units at the same $10 price. This good is best classified as

options.label: A
options.text: A normal good — demand fell when income fell

options.label: B
options.text: An inferior good — demand rose when income fell

options.label: C
options.text: A complementary good

options.label: D
options.text: A free good — its price did not change

options.label: E
options.text: A substitute good

explanation: When the consumer's income fell, her demand for this good fell (from 8 to 5 units at the same price). A decrease in income causing a decrease in demand is the defining characteristic of a normal good.

prompt: Ramen noodles are often considered an inferior good. During an economic boom when incomes are rising broadly, what would most likely happen to the demand for ramen noodles?

options.label: A
options.text: Ramen demand rises with purchasing power

options.label: B
options.text: Ramen demand falls only if its price rises

options.label: C
options.text: Ramen demand rises through complementarity with luxuries

options.label: D
options.text: Ramen demand stays unchanged because it is a staple

options.label: E
options.text: Ramen demand falls as consumers' incomes rise

explanation: Ramen noodles are an inferior good. As incomes rise during an economic boom, consumers have more purchasing power and shift toward higher-quality, more expensive food alternatives; demand for ramen decreases - the demand curve shifts leftward.

prompt: A graph shows a demand curve for concert tickets. Which of the following changes would best explain a parallel rightward shift of the entire demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: The venue reduces the number of available seats

options.label: B
options.text: The price of concert tickets rises due to higher production costs

options.label: C
options.text: The price of concert tickets falls by 20%

options.label: D
options.text: A farewell tour increases consumers' interest in concerts

options.label: E
options.text: The number of concerts produced this season decreases

explanation: A celebrity farewell announcement boosts consumer tastes and preferences for attending live concerts. This non-price demand determinant increases the demand at every price, shifting the demand curve rightward - not a price change, not a supply change.
graphDescription: Price-quantity graph for concert tickets. D₁ is the original downward-sloping demand curve. D₂ is a parallel rightward shift of D₁, indicating that at every price consumers demand more tickets than before.

prompt: The demand for electric vehicles (EVs) is affected by two simultaneous changes: (1) the price of gasoline rises, making gas-powered cars more expensive to operate, and (2) the government removes a tax credit that previously subsidized EV purchases. What is the most likely net effect on the demand for EVs?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for EVs clearly decreases because both changes reduce EV attractiveness

options.label: B
options.text: Demand for EVs clearly increases because both changes favor EVs

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for EVs is unaffected because these are supply-side changes

options.label: D
options.text: Ambiguous; higher gas prices and lost subsidies have opposing effects

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for EVs increases because higher gas prices always dominate subsidy changes

explanation: Two opposing forces affect EV demand: (1) Higher gasoline prices make gas-powered substitutes more expensive, increasing EV demand (rightward shift). (2) Removal of the tax credit raises the effective price consumers pay for EVs, decreasing EV demand (leftward shift); the net direction of the shift is ambiguous without knowing the relative magnitudes.

prompt: Smartphones and phone cases are complements. If consumer income rises and smartphones are a normal good, which of the following describes the combined effect on the demand for phone cases?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for phone cases decreases because consumers spend more on smartphones and have less to spend on accessories

options.label: B
options.text: Demand for phone cases decreases because income effects do not apply to complements

options.label: C
options.text: Case demand rises with smartphone purchases and consumers' incomes

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for phone cases is unaffected because only the smartphone market changes

options.label: E
options.text: The quantity demanded of phone cases increases due to a price drop

explanation: Both the income effect (higher income → more smartphone demand) and the complementary relationship (more smartphones purchased → more cases needed) push demand for phone cases rightward. Both determinants operate in the same direction, unambiguously increasing demand for phone cases.

prompt: A news report warns that home prices are expected to rise sharply over the next year. What would most likely happen to the current demand for homes?

options.label: A
options.text: Current housing demand rises before expected price increases

options.label: B
options.text: Current demand is unaffected because people need homes regardless

options.label: C
options.text: Current demand decreases because future prices signal lower quality

options.label: D
options.text: Current demand decreases as buyers wait to see if prices fall further

options.label: E
options.text: Current demand decreases because lenders increase interest rates in response

explanation: Consumer expectations are a demand determinant. When buyers expect prices to rise in the future, they have a strong incentive to purchase now at current prices; this increases current demand - the demand curve for homes shifts rightward.

prompt: Consumer A demands 5 units of good X at $4 and 3 units at $6. Consumer B demands 7 units at $4 and 4 units at $6. Consumer C demands 3 units at $4 and 1 unit at $6. What is the market demand at $4 and at $6?

options.label: A
options.text: $4: 15 units; $6: 6 units

options.label: B
options.text: $4: 10 units; $6: 6 units

options.label: C
options.text: $4: 7 units; $6: 4 units

options.label: D
options.text: $4: 12 units; $6: 8 units

options.label: E
options.text: $4: 15 units; $6: 8 units

explanation: At $4: 5+7+3 = 15 units; at $6: 3+4+1 = 8 units. Market demand is the horizontal sum of all individual demands at each price; the resulting market demand schedule shows 15 units at $4 and 8 units at $6.

prompt: Using the market data from Q49 (15 at $4; 8 at $6): one consumer leaves the market and no longer purchases good X. If this consumer had demanded 7 at $4 and 4 at $6, what is the new market demand?

options.label: A
options.text: $4: 8 units; $6: 4 units

options.label: B
options.text: $4: 15 units; $6: 8 units (unchanged)

options.label: C
options.text: $4: 8 units; $6: 8 units

options.label: D
options.text: $4: 22 units; $6: 12 units

options.label: E
options.text: $4: 12 units; $6: 6 units

explanation: Removing a consumer decreases market demand; new totals: At $4: 15 - 7 = 8 units. At $6: 8 - 4 = 4 units; the departure of a buyer shifts the market demand curve leftward.

prompt: A demand curve for movie theater tickets is drawn with price on the vertical axis and quantity of tickets on the horizontal axis. The following changes occur simultaneously: (1) the price of movie tickets falls by $3, and (2) a popular film franchise releases a new blockbuster. Which of the following best describes the combined effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Only the quantity demanded changes; demand itself is unaffected

options.label: B
options.text: The demand curve shifts rightward only

options.label: C
options.text: The demand curve shifts leftward because lower prices reduce producer incentives

options.label: D
options.text: There is only a movement along the demand curve

options.label: E
options.text: Demand shifts right; the lower price increases quantity along the new curve

explanation: Two effects occur simultaneously: (1) The price of movie tickets falls → movement down and to the right along the demand curve (more quantity demanded at the lower price). (2) A new blockbuster increases consumer preferences for movies → rightward shift of the demand curve; both a shift and a movement occur.

prompt: The market for streaming services has two current subscribers: Ali (demands 2 subscriptions at $15/month) and Ben (demands 1 at $15/month). A third subscriber, Carla, enters who demands 3 at $15/month. How does this affect the market demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand shifts right; quantity at $15 rises from 3 to 6

options.label: B
options.text: There is a movement along the demand curve to a higher price

options.label: C
options.text: The demand curve shifts rightward because the number of buyers increased; total market demand at $15 rises from 3 to 6

options.label: D
options.text: The demand curve shifts leftward because there are now more alternatives in the market

options.label: E
options.text: No change — the demand curve only shifts when prices change

explanation: An increase in the number of buyers is a demand determinant. With Carla entering, market quantity demanded at $15 rises from 2+1=3 to 2+1+3=6; this shifts the market demand curve rightward; (E is equivalent to C here - the most precise description.).

prompt: Assume coffee is a normal good and tea is a substitute for coffee. Which combination of changes would unambiguously shift the demand curve for coffee to the RIGHT?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumer income increases; price of tea rises

options.label: B
options.text: Consumer income decreases; price of tea rises

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer income increases; price of tea falls

options.label: D
options.text: Consumer income decreases; price of tea falls

options.label: E
options.text: Number of buyers decreases; consumer income increases

explanation: Two forces both increase coffee demand: (1) Higher consumer income → more demand for coffee (normal good). (2) Higher tea price → some consumers switch to coffee (substitute effect); both determinants reinforce each other, unambiguously shifting the coffee demand curve rightward.

prompt: Assume generic cereal is an inferior good and brand-name cereal is a substitute. If consumer income decreases, which of the following best describes the combined effect on demand for generic cereal?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for generic cereal is unchanged because both effects cancel

options.label: B
options.text: Lower incomes and pricier substitutes both raise generic-cereal demand

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for generic cereal decreases because income fell

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for generic cereal decreases because generic goods always have lower quality

options.label: E
options.text: The quantity demanded of generic cereal decreases due to a movement along its demand curve

explanation: Lower income has two demand-increasing effects on generic cereal: (1) As an inferior good, lower income directly increases demand for generic cereal. (2) Lower income also makes brand-name cereal less affordable, pushing consumers toward cheaper generic alternatives (substitute effect); both effects increase demand for generic cereal - rightward shift.

prompt: Economists distinguish between individual demand and market demand. Which of the following best explains how the market demand curve is constructed from individual demand curves?

options.label: A
options.text: By vertically summing all individual demand curves — adding prices at each quantity level

options.label: B
options.text: By multiplying each individual demand quantity by the price level

options.label: C
options.text: Adding consumers' quantities demanded at each price

options.label: D
options.text: By averaging the price levels of all individual demand curves

options.label: E
options.text: By selecting the individual demand curve with the largest quantity demanded

explanation: Market demand is derived by horizontal summation of individual demand curves. At each price level, the quantities demanded by all individual consumers are added together; this produces the market demand curve showing total quantity demanded at each price.

prompt: A consumer switches from buying store-brand orange juice to name-brand orange juice after receiving a significant pay raise. This behavior indicates that store-brand orange juice is most likely

options.label: A
options.text: A normal good, because demand increased with income

options.label: B
options.text: An inferior good, with demand falling as income rises

options.label: C
options.text: A complement to name-brand orange juice

options.label: D
options.text: A normal good for which the price fell

options.label: E
options.text: A substitute for name-brand juice that experienced a price increase

explanation: The consumer reduced consumption of store-brand juice when income rose - this is the hallmark of an inferior good. The consumer was buying store-brand as a lower-cost substitute, and once income rose, she switched to the preferred, higher-quality brand-name option.

prompt: Two goods, X and Y, are related such that when the price of X rises, consumers buy more of Y. This relationship indicates that X and Y are

options.label: A
options.text: Normal goods — both goods have positive income effects

options.label: B
options.text: Substitute goods — consumers switch to Y when X becomes more expensive

options.label: C
options.text: Independent goods — changes in X's price do not affect Y

options.label: D
options.text: Complementary goods — consumed together

options.label: E
options.text: Inferior goods — both decrease in demand when income rises

explanation: When the price of X rises and consumers buy more of Y, X and Y are substitute goods. Consumers switch from the now-more-expensive X to Y, increasing demand for Y; this is the defining relationship of substitutes.

prompt: Two goods, A and B, are related such that when the price of A falls, the demand for B also decreases. This relationship indicates that A and B are

options.label: A
options.text: Inferior goods — both demand less when prices fall

options.label: B
options.text: Complementary goods — a fall in A's price increases purchases of A, and since B is used with A, demand for B rises, not falls

options.label: C
options.text: Complementary goods — they are used together, so more A purchased means less B needed separately

options.label: D
options.text: Independent goods

options.label: E
options.text: Substitutes; cheaper A reduces purchases of B

explanation: When the price of A falls and demand for B decreases, A and B are substitutes. Cheaper A attracts buyers away from B - they substitute A for B - decreasing the demand for B; this is the classic substitute relationship.

prompt: Identify the likely relationship (complement or substitute) between each pair: (1) smartphones and data plans; (2) iPhones and Android phones; (3) butter and margarine.

options.label: A
options.text: (1) substitute; (2) complement; (3) substitute

options.label: B
options.text: (1) substitute; (2) substitute; (3) complement

options.label: C
options.text: (1) complement; (2) substitute; (3) complement

options.label: D
options.text: (1) complement; (2) substitute; (3) substitute

options.label: E
options.text: (1) complement; (2) complement; (3) substitute

explanation: (1) Smartphones and data plans are complements - a smartphone is nearly useless without a data plan. (2) iPhones and Android phones are substitutes - both serve the same function and consumers choose between them; (3) Butter and margarine are substitutes - both serve the same culinary purpose and consumers switch between them based on price and preference.

prompt: A demand curve for new housing shifts significantly rightward over 5 years in a growing city. Which combination of factors could BEST explain this sustained rightward shift?

options.label: A
options.text: A consistent decline in housing prices over the 5-year period

options.label: B
options.text: Higher incomes, more buyers, and expected property-price increases

options.label: C
options.text: A series of interest rate increases that raise mortgage costs

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in consumer income combined with fewer buyers in the market

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in construction activity that raises the supply of houses

explanation: A sustained rightward shift of demand requires ongoing changes in demand determinants: rising incomes (normal good effect), population growth (more buyers), and positive price expectations (buy now to avoid higher future prices) all simultaneously increase demand, explaining a sustained multi-year rightward shift.

prompt: A demand graph for gasoline shows the demand curve shifting leftward. Which of the following demand determinants could BEST explain this shift?

options.label: A
options.text: Consumers replace gasoline vehicles with electric vehicles

options.label: B
options.text: An increase in consumer income, as gasoline is a normal good

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in the number of drivers on the road

options.label: D
options.text: A decrease in the price of gasoline

options.label: E
options.text: An increase in gasoline prices due to higher crude oil costs

explanation: A large shift toward electric vehicles reduces the number of buyers in the gasoline market (fewer gas-powered car owners). This is a non-price demand determinant - fewer buyers means lower total market demand at every price, shifting the gasoline demand curve leftward.

prompt: A government announces it will impose a large tax on cigarettes starting next month, which will significantly raise cigarette prices. What would most likely happen to the CURRENT demand for cigarettes before the tax takes effect?

options.label: A
options.text: Current demand is unaffected because tobacco is an addictive good with no substitute

options.label: B
options.text: Current demand is unchanged because the tax has not yet been implemented

options.label: C
options.text: Current demand rises before the anticipated tax increase

options.label: D
options.text: Current demand decreases because cigarettes become an inferior good

options.label: E
options.text: Current demand decreases because consumers are afraid of higher future costs

explanation: Consumer expectations about future price increases are a demand determinant. Knowing prices will rise next month gives consumers an incentive to stock up now - increasing current demand and shifting the current demand curve rightward.

prompt: The market demand schedule for bicycles shows: at $200, 500 bikes demanded; at $300, 400 bikes demanded; at $400, 300 bikes demanded. A new bike-sharing program reduces the number of individual bike buyers by 20%. If each remaining buyer's demand is unchanged, which of the following describes the new market demand at $200?

options.label: A
options.text: 400 bikes

options.label: B
options.text: 600 bikes

options.label: C
options.text: 300 bikes

options.label: D
options.text: 250 bikes

options.label: E
options.text: 500 bikes (unchanged)

explanation: A 20% reduction in the number of buyers reduces total market quantity demanded proportionally at each price. At $200: 500 × (1 - 0.20) = 500 × 0.80 = 400 bikes; fewer buyers shift the market demand curve leftward.

prompt: Which of the following pairs of changes would cause an ambiguous (uncertain) net shift in the demand curve for a normal good?

options.label: A
options.text: The number of buyers decreases AND a competing substitute good becomes more expensive

options.label: B
options.text: Consumer income rises AND the number of buyers increases

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer income rises AND a substitute good becomes cheaper

options.label: D
options.text: Consumer income falls AND consumer preferences shift away from the good

options.label: E
options.text: Consumer expectations become more optimistic AND consumer income rises

explanation: When consumer income rises (increases demand for a normal good) but a substitute becomes cheaper (reduces demand by drawing consumers away), the two effects work in opposite directions. Without knowing which effect is larger, the net change in demand is ambiguous.

prompt: A consumer's demand curve for a luxury watch shifts leftward by exactly the same amount as a different consumer's demand curve shifts rightward. What is the net effect on the market demand curve for luxury watches?

options.label: A
options.text: The market demand curve shifts rightward

options.label: B
options.text: The market demand curve shifts leftward

options.label: C
options.text: The market demand curve disappears because demand is zero

options.label: D
options.text: The equal opposing shifts leave market demand unchanged

options.label: E
options.text: The market demand curve rotates, becoming steeper

explanation: Market demand is the horizontal sum of all individual demands. If one consumer's demand decreases by exactly the same amount that another's increases, the changes cancel perfectly - total market quantity demanded at every price is unchanged, and the market demand curve does not shift.

prompt: Consumers expect their incomes to rise significantly next year due to announced wage increases. How does this expectation affect their current demand for durable goods (like appliances and electronics)?

options.label: A
options.text: Current demand decreases because consumers save in anticipation of future spending

options.label: B
options.text: Current demand is unaffected because income has not yet changed

options.label: C
options.text: Current demand decreases because higher future income means consumers will buy better goods later

options.label: D
options.text: Current demand decreases because durable goods are inferior goods

options.label: E
options.text: Expected higher income increases willingness to spend now

explanation: Consumer expectations - including expectations about future income - are a demand determinant. When consumers expect income to rise, they feel wealthier and more confident, often increasing current spending on durable goods; this shifts current demand rightward.

prompt: The demand for smartphones increases significantly in a country where many new buyers enter the market for the first time due to falling smartphone prices. A student says this is a "shift of the demand curve." Is the student correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Yes — falling smartphone prices change consumer income, which is a demand determinant

options.label: B
options.text: No — only income changes can shift the demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: Yes — new buyers entering the market is a separate demand determinant that shifts the curve

options.label: D
options.text: Yes — any increase in the quantity of smartphones purchased represents a demand shift

options.label: E
options.text: No; its own-price decrease increases quantity along existing demand

explanation: The student is incorrect about the mechanism; falling smartphone prices cause a movement along the existing demand curve - a change in quantity demanded; the demand curve itself does not shift.

prompt:
The table below shows the demand schedule for concert tickets. Identify whether each event causes a shift of the demand curve or a movement along it.

Event 1: Ticket prices fall from $80 to $60.
Event 2: Consumer incomes rise by 15%.
Event 3: A competing entertainment venue closes permanently.

options.label: A
options.text: All three events cause shifts of the demand curve

options.label: B
options.text: Event 1: movement along curve; Event 2: movement along curve; Event 3: shift right

options.label: C
options.text: Event 1: shift left; Event 2: shift right; Event 3: shift right

options.label: D
options.text: Event 1: shift right; Event 2: shift right; Event 3: movement along curve

options.label: E
options.text: Event 1: movement; events 2 and 3: rightward shifts

explanation: Event 1: Price falls → movement along the demand curve (increase in quantity demanded). Event 2: Higher incomes → demand determinant change → demand shifts right (concerts are normal); event 3: Fewer alternatives → competing venue closes, increasing consumers' relative preference for concerts → demand shifts right.

prompt: A graph shows the demand curve for a product. After a change in consumer income, the demand curve shifts from D₁ to D₂ where D₂ lies entirely to the LEFT of D₁. Which of the following is most consistent with this graph if the product is a normal good?

options.label: A
options.text: The price of a complement decreased, shifting demand leftward

options.label: B
options.text: The price of the good fell, causing a movement along the curve

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer income decreased, reducing demand for this normal good at every price

options.label: D
options.text: Consumer expectations became more pessimistic about future income

options.label: E
options.text: Consumer income increased

explanation: For a normal good, a decrease in consumer income reduces demand - less is purchased at every price. This is shown as a leftward shift from D₁ to D₂; the leftward shift is consistent with a fall in income for a normal good.
graphDescription: Price-quantity graph showing two downward-sloping demand curves. D₁ is the original, D₂ is to the left of D₁ (parallel leftward shift), indicating lower quantity demanded at every price after the income change.

prompt: Hot chocolate and whipped cream are complements. During a severe winter, demand for hot chocolate increases significantly. What most likely happens to the demand for whipped cream?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for whipped cream decreases because winter weather makes it harder to produce

options.label: B
options.text: Whipped-cream demand rises with consumption of complementary hot chocolate

options.label: C
options.text: Demand for whipped cream increases only if the price of whipped cream also falls

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for whipped cream decreases because consumer incomes fall in winter

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for whipped cream is unaffected because its own price did not change

explanation: Whipped cream is a complement to hot chocolate. As demand for hot chocolate increases (more is being consumed), consumers also demand more whipped cream to use with it; the demand for the complement (whipped cream) shifts rightward.

prompt: A consumer has the following individual demand schedule for energy drinks: $1→8 cans; $2→6 cans; $3→4 cans; $4→2 cans. After a fitness trend causes the consumer to lose interest in energy drinks, the new demand schedule is: $1→4 cans; $2→3 cans; $3→2 cans; $4→1 can. What type of change occurred and what caused it?

options.label: A
options.text: A shift of the demand curve to the right caused by a change in preferences

options.label: B
options.text: A shift of the demand curve to the left caused by an increase in the price of energy drinks

options.label: C
options.text: A leftward shift as preferences for energy drinks weaken

options.label: D
options.text: A movement along the demand curve caused by a price change

options.label: E
options.text: A movement along the demand curve caused by a reduction in income

explanation: At every price, the consumer now demands fewer cans than before - the demand curve has shifted leftward. This is caused by a change in consumer preferences (fitness trend reducing appeal of energy drinks), which is a demand determinant; the price did not change - this is a shift, not a movement.

prompt: Tea is an inferior good in Country X. The country experiences rapid economic growth that raises average consumer incomes by 25%. Which of the following MOST accurately predicts the effect on the demand for tea in Country X?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand for tea increases because higher income means consumers can afford more of all goods

options.label: B
options.text: The quantity demanded of tea decreases due to a movement along the demand curve

options.label: C
options.text: Tea demand falls as higher-income consumers choose other beverages

options.label: D
options.text: Demand for tea increases because tea becomes relatively cheaper after incomes rise

options.label: E
options.text: Demand for tea is unchanged because tea is a staple that income does not affect

explanation: Tea is an inferior good in Country X. As consumer incomes rise by 25%, consumers have more purchasing power and shift toward preferred, higher-quality beverages (the income effect for an inferior good); demand for tea decreases - the demand curve shifts leftward.

prompt: Which of the following correctly identifies all five standard determinants of demand that can shift the demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: Income, related prices, preferences, buyer numbers, and expectations

options.label: B
options.text: Consumer income; prices of substitutes only; producer expectations; number of buyers; tastes

options.label: C
options.text: Consumer income; input prices; prices of related goods; number of buyers; tastes

options.label: D
options.text: Price of the good; consumer income; prices of related goods; number of sellers; technology

options.label: E
options.text: Price level; consumer income; taxes; number of producers; consumer preferences

explanation: The five standard determinants of demand (non-price factors that shift the demand curve) are: (1) consumer income, (2) prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), (3) consumer tastes and preferences, (4) number of buyers in the market, and (5) consumer expectations about future prices or income.

prompt: Good Z is simultaneously a normal good for high-income consumers and an inferior good for low-income consumers. If an economic boom raises both high-income and low-income consumers' incomes, which of the following best describes the net effect on the demand for Good Z?

options.label: A
options.text: Demand unambiguously increases because all incomes rose

options.label: B
options.text: Demand is unaffected because the two income effects exactly cancel in all cases

options.label: C
options.text: Demand unambiguously decreases because most consumers are low-income

options.label: D
options.text: Demand increases only if the price of Good Z falls simultaneously

options.label: E
options.text: Ambiguous; the groups' opposing responses depend on size and income sensitivity

explanation: When a good is normal for some consumers and inferior for others, rising income has opposite effects on different market segments. High-income consumers (who see Z as normal) demand more; low-income consumers (who see Z as inferior) demand less; without knowing the sizes of these groups and their income sensitivities, the net direction of the demand shift is ambiguous.

prompt: The demand curve for a good slopes downward due to two reinforcing effects when price falls. Which pair of effects correctly explains the downward slope of the demand curve?

options.label: A
options.text: The cost effect and the revenue effect: lower prices reduce costs and increase revenue simultaneously

options.label: B
options.text: The wealth effect and the expectation effect: lower prices increase wealth and improve expectations

options.label: C
options.text: The scale effect and the scope effect: larger purchase volumes reduce unit costs

options.label: D
options.text: The labor effect and the capital effect: lower prices reduce input costs for firms

options.label: E
options.text: Lower prices raise purchasing power and encourage substitution toward the good

explanation: The downward slope of the demand curve is explained by two reinforcing effects when price falls: (1) The income effect - a lower price increases the consumer's real purchasing power, allowing more purchases. (2) The substitution effect - a lower price makes the good relatively cheaper compared to substitutes, so consumers substitute toward it; both effects increase quantity demanded.

prompt: Good A and Good B are substitutes. Good B and Good C are complements. If the price of Good A rises, trace the full chain of effects on the demand for Good C.

options.label: A
options.text: Price of A rises → demand for B decreases (as A's complement) → demand for C falls

options.label: B
options.text: Price of A rises → demand for A decreases → demand for B decreases → demand for C decreases

options.label: C
options.text: Higher A prices increase B demand, which increases complementary C demand

options.label: D
options.text: Price of A rises → demand for A increases → demand for B increases → demand for C falls

options.label: E
options.text: Price of A rises → demand for A decreases → no effect on B or C because indirect effects are negligible

explanation: Chain of effects: (1) Price of A rises → consumers substitute away from A toward B (substitutes), so demand for B increases. (2) B and C are complements - more B purchased means more C demanded alongside it; therefore, the demand for C increases; the chain goes: A price ↑ → B demand ↑ (substitution) → C demand ↑ (complementarity).

prompt: The market demand for housing in a city is shaped by multiple simultaneous changes: (1) population grows by 10% due to in-migration, (2) average consumer income rises by 8%, (3) consumers expect housing prices to rise 15% next year, (4) the price of a substitute (renting) also rises. Assuming housing is a normal good, what is the most likely net effect on current housing demand?

options.label: A
options.text: Changes 2 and 4 increase demand; changes 1 and 3 are irrelevant to demand

options.label: B
options.text: All four changes increase current housing demand

options.label: C
options.text: Only change 1 (population growth) affects demand; the others affect supply

options.label: D

prompt: A consumer's demand for a good rises even though the price of that good increased. Without invoking supply-side factors, which of the following demand-side explanations is most consistent with the law of demand?

explanation: The law of demand is not violated; if a demand determinant changes (e.g., income rises or preferences improve), the entire demand curve shifts rightward. If the rightward shift is large enough, consumers may demand MORE of the good at the new (higher) price than they demanded at the old (lower) price on the original demand curve. Both the law of demand (movement along the new curve) and a demand shift are consistent with this observation.

prompt: A market has 200 consumers each with demand Qd = 8 − 2P (active for P ≤ $4). A new product becomes fashionable, shifting each consumer's demand to Qd = 12 − 2P. prompt: A student argues: "Because the demand curve is always downward sloping, it is impossible for total spending on a good to increase when price rises." Evaluate this claim strictly using law of demand principles.

However, total spending = P × Qd, and whether it rises or falls depends on which effect dominates; if price rises 10% and quantity falls only 5%, total spending increases. The law of demand governs the direction of quantity change only - not total expenditure; (This touches elasticity concepts but the core logic is grounded in the law of demand.).

prompt: Which of the following best explains why the market demand curve is flatter (more elastic) than any individual consumer's demand curve for the same good?
